doc.title: Buddy DeFranco interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 13, 1996

title: The clarinet as an 'agony pipe'
summary: DeFranco explains his sister's name for the clarinet and agrees with Rowe that it is among the hardest instruments, with too many mediocre jazz clarinetists.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: We are filming today for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive and it’s a great pleasure to have with us master clarinetist Buddy DeFranco, who just described his instrument as an “agony pipe.”
I got that from my sister Maryanne. Maryanne always called it an agony pipe. She says that’s what it sounded like when I was practicing. And she was right. It’s the strangest instrument.
Difficult. One of the more difficult instruments I think.
Difficult, and I would say in line with the bassoon, oboe, French horn and harp. It’s in that category. It’s agonizing. You must squeak on a clarinet for years before you begin to play anything.
And it strikes me like a violin in that there is no such thing as a mediocre violin or clarinet. It’s either you’re really good or if it’s mediocre it’s awful.
It’s pretty bad. We’ve got a problem though in jazz, of too many mediocre clarinet players who insist on playing.

Yeah. Well they figure I can play sax, I can play clarinet. Well you’ve had quite an interesting career and we want to talk about some of the things you’ve done. Didn’t you start out winning a contest?
